The first cloth hall here was a double row of stone stalls, with a little lane down the middle.
At night, that lane was locked at both ends.
The prince had promised these stone stalls as early as 1257, when the town was founded.
Around 1300, the passage between the stalls was roofed, and it began to look like a market hall.
Before 1358, the king built a new Gothic hall here, 108 metres long.
In 1601, a passage was cut across the hall.
Between 1875 and 1879, it was rebuilt once more, and the stalls and buildings around it were pulled down.
Some of the carved masks on the gables are caricatures of two mayors of Kraków, made to a design by Jan Matejko.
The gallery upstairs opened on October 7, 1879.

The hall has hosted many distinguished guests, among them Emperor Akihito of Japan, who was welcomed here in 2002.
In 1809, balls were held here after Prince Poniatowski had briefly liberated the city from the Austrians.

There, visitors walk on glass ramps and footbridges above the old roads, including the paving of the medieval cloth hall.

sentences: You're standing at the Cloth Hall, the central feature of the Main Market Square.
It was once a major centre of international trade.
Travelling merchants met here to discuss business and to barter.
In its golden age, in the 15th century, the hall was the source of exotic imports from the east: spices, silk, leather and wax.
Kraków itself exported textiles, lead and salt.
The Gothic hall burned down in 1555.
When it was rebuilt, it was crowned with an arcaded parapet, decorated with carved masks.
The building you see dates to the Renaissance, and it is one of the most recognizable monuments of the city.
In the 19th century, its successful renovation was one of the most notable achievements of a period of revival.
On the upper floor is a branch of the National Museum, with the largest permanent exhibit of 19th-century Polish painting and sculpture.
And the hall is still used as a centre of commerce today.
Before you walk on, find the carved masks along the parapet on the roof line.

The church you see is not the first on this spot.
According to the chronicler Jan Długosz, the first church was founded in 1221 by the Bishop of Kraków.
That building was destroyed during the Mongol invasion of Poland.
Between 1290 and 1300, a new early Gothic church was built on the remaining foundations.
It was consecrated in 1320.
During the reign of Casimir the Great, the church was completely rebuilt, and tall windows were added.
In the first half of the 15th century, the northern tower was raised to serve as the watch tower for the entire city.
A gilded crown was placed on its helmet in 1666, and it is still there today.
At the end of the 15th century, the church received its sculptural masterpiece, the late Gothic altarpiece of Veit Stoss.
It stands behind the high altar, and it was carved between 1477 and 1489.
Veit Stoss was a German-born sculptor, who lived and worked in this city for over 20 years.
Today the altarpiece is a national treasure of Poland.
In 1536, King Sigismund declared that the sermons here should be given in Polish instead of German.
The large German community then moved its worship to the smaller Saint Barbara's church.
In the 18th century, the interior was rebuilt in the late Baroque style.
All 26 altars were replaced, and the walls were decorated with painting.
At the beginning of the 19th century, a cemetery near the basilica was closed and replaced by a public square.
Between 1887 and 1891, the church gained its neo-Gothic design, with murals painted and funded by Jan Matejko.
He worked with two other artists, the authors of the stained glass in the presbytery.
The basilica also served as a model for many churches built by the Polish diaspora abroad, among them two in Chicago.
Listen once more for the trumpet from the taller tower before you go.

sentences: You're standing before Saint Mary's Basilica, a Brick Gothic church at the corner of the Main Market Square.
It was built in the 14th century, on foundations from the early 13th century.
Every hour, day and night, a trumpet signal is played from the top of the taller of its two towers.
Listen to the end, because the plaintive tune breaks off in mid-stream.
The story behind it is of a trumpeter, shot in the throat while he sounded the alarm before a Mongol attack.
The first account of that story comes from an American novel of 1928, The Trumpeter of Krakow.
At noon, the call is broadcast live by Polish Radio, and it is heard across Poland and abroad.
The church is most famous for its wooden altarpiece, carved by Veit Stoss.
Some of its painted murals were designed by Jan Matejko, the leading history painter of Poland.
In 1978, the church became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, together with the Historic Centre of Kraków.
Before you walk on, look once more at the taller tower, and wait for the next call.

You're standing at Saint Andrew's Church, one of the oldest buildings in Kraków.
It is a Romanesque church, built between 1079 and 1098 by a medieval Polish statesman.
It is also a rare surviving example of a fortress church, used for defence.
Along the lower part of its facade, look for the small openings.
They served as defensive windows, at a time when the church was a place of refuge.
In 1241 it was the only church in Kraków to withstand the Mongol attack.
It gave shelter to most of the people of the city.
At that time it was called the lower castle, to set it apart from the upper one on Wawel Hill.
From 1320, the church belonged to the Order of Poor Clares.
The Baroque domes on top of its two octagonal towers were added in 1639.
Inside, the Baroque decoration includes a pulpit in the shape of a boat.
Before you walk on, look again at the two towers.
Their Baroque domes contrast with the severe Romanesque form of the church below.

You're standing at Saint Florian's Gate, one of the best-known Polish Gothic towers.
The tower is thirty-three and a half metres tall, and its Baroque metal helmet, made in 1660, adds another metre.
The tower was first mentioned in 1307.
It was part of a rampart built around the city after the Tatar attack of 1241, which destroyed most of Kraków.
At its height, the wall had 47 watchtowers and eight gates.
This is the only one of those gates that was not dismantled in the 19th century.
The Royal Route begins here.
Through this gate came kings and princes, foreign envoys and distinguished guests, parades and coronation processions.
They travelled up Saint Florian's Street to the Main Market Square, and on up Castle Street to Wawel Castle.
Today, you follow in their footsteps.
Before you walk on, look for the carvings on the tower.
One face bears a stone eagle, carved in 1882 to a design by the painter Jan Matejko.
The other face shows Saint Florian himself, in a relief from the 18th century.

The massive Gothic tower was built of stone and brick at the end of the 14th century.
It stands 70 metres tall.
It also leans by 55 centimetres, the result of a storm in 1703.
In 1680, lightning set fire to its original Gothic helmet.
The royal architect then designed a new and imposing Baroque helmet, which survived only until 1783.
When it began to crumble, it was replaced by a smaller structure.
Its cellars once housed a city prison, with a medieval torture chamber.
At the top, an observation deck is open to visitors, with a panoramic view of the city.
Before you walk on, look at the entrance.
It is guarded by a pair of stone lions, under the original Gothic portal with the city coat of arms.

You're standing before the Church of Saints Peter and Paul, on Grodzka Street.
This street is part of the Royal Route, used by Polish kings to reach Wawel Castle.
The church is the first structure in Kraków designed entirely in the Baroque style.
It was funded by King Sigismund Vasa for the Jesuit order, and it was built between 1597 and 1619.
Of all the historic churches of Kraków, it has the largest number of seats.
In front of the church, sculptures of the apostles stand on their plinths.
The originals were completed in 1722, and acid rain damaged them badly.
What you see today are contemporary copies, made of the same stone.
The facade is built of dolomite, and its very top carries the coat of arms of the Vasa dynasty.
Inside hangs the longest Foucault pendulum in Poland.
Every Thursday, it is demonstrated as a simple proof that the Earth rotates.
The pendulum weighs 25 kilograms, and its red laser marks a clock face on the floor.
In the basement beneath the floor of the church, the priest Piotr Skarga is buried.
Before you walk on, look again at the apostles, each on its own plinth.

Wawel's oldest stone buildings can be traced back to 970.
The hill also holds the earliest examples of Romanesque and Gothic architecture in Poland.
Some of the oldest remains are those of the Rotunda of the Virgin Mary.
The castle you see was built in the 14th century.
Over the next hundreds of years, it was enlarged into a number of buildings around a Renaissance courtyard.
The limestone of the hill abounds in caves, and one of them is the Dragon's Den.
At the foot of the hill, in front of the den, stands a dragon statue, installed in 1972.
It can let out fire from its mouth, and usually does so every 15 minutes.
One theory links the name Wawel to a Polish word that means ravine.
A ravine once divided the hill.
Archaeological remains show settlement on the hill from the 4th century.
In the 10th century, the lands of the Vistulans and Kraków became part of the emerging state of Poland.
For most of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, Wawel was the seat of the national government and the Diet, the assembly.
As the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth formed and grew, Wawel became the seat of one of the largest states in Europe.
That status was lost when the capital was moved to Warsaw in 1596.
From the late 18th century, Wawel was the setting for gatherings of people from Kraków, protesting against the foreign occupation.
Sigismund's Chapel, a royal chapel of the cathedral, was built from 1519 as a funerary chapel for the last members of the Jagiellonian dynasty.
In the crypt of the national bards, beneath the cathedral, lies the poet Adam Mickiewicz, whose monument stands in the Main Market Square.
The castle is now one of the country's premier art museums, established in 1930.
Its collections include Italian Renaissance paintings and the tapestries of Sigismund Augustus.
Its oriental art includes the largest collection of Ottoman tents in Europe.
In 2025, it was the most visited art museum in Poland.

You're standing in front of the Barbican, a fortified outpost and a historic gateway into the Old Town.
It is a round brick structure, ringed by a moat and crowned with seven turrets.
Its walls are three metres thick, and they hold 130 embrasures.
The city built it around 1498, fearing an attack by the Ottoman Empire.
It is one of only three such outposts still surviving in Europe, and the best preserved.
A covered passage once linked it to the city walls, through Saint Florian's Gate.
It served as a checkpoint for everyone who entered the city.
Early in the 19th century, the Barbican was threatened with demolition.
In 1817, two senators of the Free City of Kraków convinced the Senate to preserve it.
Today it belongs to the Historical Museum of the City of Kraków, and you can tour its interior.
Before you move on, count its seven turrets.

You're walking along Kanonicza Street, a historic street of the Old Town.

Number 25, at the foot of Wawel hill, is the Długosz House, built in the 14th century.

You're standing at the Church of Saint Adalbert, one of the oldest stone churches in Poland.
Its history goes back almost a thousand years, to the beginning of Polish Romanesque architecture.
Merchants travelling from across Europe came here to worship.
The church was built in the 11th century, and it is named after the martyred missionary Saint Adalbert.
It is older than the square itself, by nearly a century.
The square was laid out in 1257, and it is the biggest medieval market square in Europe.
Over the centuries, new pavement raised the level of the square by 2 to 2.6 metres.
That is why the floor of the church lies below the present level of the square.
In the 17th century, its walls were raised, and it was topped with a new Baroque dome.
The crypt holds a small museum of the history of the Market Square.
In the 1960s, the earliest church was discovered here, dating back to the times when Saint Adalbert lived in Kraków.
Before you walk on, notice how the door opens directly into the noise of the square.
